title: Edit a year into a photo book, not a camera roll
description: Choose a clear story for a year of photographs, add dates and captions, and protect original prints or files while preparing the book.
intent: How do I select and organize photographs from one year into a readable book without trying to include every image?

sections.heading: Pick the story before the photographs
paragraphs: A year is too large to tell one image at a time. Choose a simple frame: one home, one project, a changing season, a year with a particular person, or the ordinary routines that held the months together. The frame helps you choose, and it lets the book show more than holidays and posed portraits.

Start with a folder or contact sheet of candidates. Include different kinds of images: people, places, meals, objects, weather, a familiar route and small changes in a room. Keep photos that make you remember a moment, not only the technically sharp ones. If other people appear, think about their privacy before printing or sharing the book.

sections.heading: Build a sequence with breathing room
paragraphs: Sort the images into months or chapters, then look for an opening and ending that make sense. You might begin with the first week, a place you returned to, or an object that appears across the year. Alternate busy spreads with quieter pages. A book that contains every good photograph can become harder to read than a tighter selection.

Limit each spread to a small number of images and give some photographs room to stand alone. If several pictures show nearly the same moment, choose the one that tells the story best. Keep a separate archive folder for the images you do not print; editing the book does not mean deleting the rest.

sections.heading: Add captions that recover context
paragraphs: A short caption can record who, where, when and why a photograph matters. Avoid describing only what is visible. “Three cups on the table” may be obvious; “first breakfast after the move, before the boxes were unpacked” gives future readers context. If a date or name is uncertain, mark it as an estimate rather than filling the gap with a guess.

Ask someone in the image how they would like to be identified, and consider leaving out private or painful details. A caption can protect dignity as well as preserve memory. You do not need to explain every photograph; leave some space for a person looking at the book to bring their own memory.

sections.heading: Handle originals with care
paragraphs: If you are including old prints, do not glue, tape or write directly on the image. The Library of Congress advises handling photographs by their edges, avoiding adhesives and choosing photo-safe albums rather than sticky or magnetic pages. For a new photo book, use scans or duplicate prints when you can, and keep fragile originals in suitable protective storage.

Digital images need their own simple organization. Keep the original files and a backup, and use copies for cropping or color adjustments. If you order a printed book, check the proof for captions, sequence and page edges before approving it. Product-specific print requirements vary, so follow the provider’s current specifications rather than relying on a generic template.

sections.heading: Make the first edition finishable
paragraphs: Set a practical cap for the project: a fixed number of pages, a maximum number of images per month, or one selection session each weekend. You can make a smaller first book and leave a note about what you excluded. The goal is a readable record of the year, not a complete archive in one volume.

After printing, write the year and the book’s frame on the inside cover. Store it away from direct sunlight, damp and high-traffic handling. Keep the digital source folder organized so you can revisit it later. Your next step is to choose the story in one sentence and make a first shortlist of photographs from three different months.

sources.title: Care, Handling, and Storage of Photographs
sources.purpose: Supports edge handling, avoiding adhesives on prints, photo-safe albums and protective storage; digital files require separate guidance.
